To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the effect of the transfer price rule inconsistency probability on the firm's expected tax payment depends on the relative magnitudes of the tax rate differential and the transfer price rule consistency probability; 2) the effect of transfer price rule consistency on the tax authorities' expected audit costs depends on the magnitude of the tax rate difference; and 3) the transfer price rule probability has no effect on the tax authorities expected audit costs when the tax rate difference is zero.

the probability of transfer pricing rule inconsistency has an ambiguous effect on taxpayer reporting and tax authorities' audit strategies and that it can either increase or decease the taxpayer's expected liability and the expected deadweight loss from audits.
an increase in inconsistent transfer price rules can increase or decrease a firm's expected taxes, and that an increase in such rules can increase or decease the deadweight loss of auditing.

the effect of the transfer pricing rules on taxpayer reporting and tax authorities audit strategies in an environment with information asymmetry.
the effects of the probability of inconsistent transfer pricing rules on the strategies of taxpayers and tax authorities in an international setting.
the strategic interactions among multinational taxpayers, tax authorities, and the transfer price rules that the tax authorities use.

the effects of inconsistent transfer price rules are ambiguous and that the net effect of the inconsistency depends on the parameters of the model.

the effect of transfer price rule inconsistencies depends on the specific circumstances and the specific transfer pricing rule in question.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the probability of transfer pricing rule inconsistency affects the taxpayer's reporting and tax authorities' auditing strategies in a complicated manner.

the probability of transfer pricing rule inconsistency can either increase or reduce the taxpayer's expected income reported, the taxpayer's expected transfer pricing tax liability, and the expected audit costs of the two tax authorities.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the effect of transfer price rule inconsistencies on a firm's expected liability depends on how the firm's tax compliance strategies respond to the probability of transfer pricing rule inconsistency.
the impact of transfer price rule inconsistencies on the taxpayer's behavior, and hence the taxpayer's expected income tax liability and governments’ audit costs, is an empirical question.

it is not the prospect of double tax but the prospect of inconsistent transfer pricing rules that is the key determinant of the taxpayer's and tax authorities' reporting and audit strategies in a multinational tax setting.
